editorial_candidates.excerpt: The spherical Coxeter complex is a triangulation of S^2 with 24 triangular chambers, 36 edges and 14 vertices; the vertex types split 4+6+4, and links of selected parabolic vertices are cycles of length 6 or 4.
editorial_candidates.classification: source-supported editorial candidate; no mathematical defect asserted
editorial_candidates.why_warranted: The source supplies a dense global incidence count and two distinct local residue cycles. A single schematic would let readers see how the 24 chambers, 14 vertices, and parabolic links fit together.
editorial_candidates.specific_content: Use the combinatorial model as the barycentric subdivision of a tetrahedron boundary: 4 vertices from one-vertex subsets, 6 from two-vertex subsets, and 4 from three-vertex subsets; its flags give 24 triangular faces and its edges total 36. Highlight one vertex in a size-6 or size-4 coset class and its link cycle (hexagon for I={s2,s3} or square for I={s1,s3}). Mark this as a combinatorial schematic, not a metric spherical tetrahedron or metric identification beyond the source claim.
editorial_candidates.mathematical_check: The item gives |W|=24, rank-two subgroup orders 6,4,6 and hence vertex orbit sizes 4,6,4 (lines 36-48, supported by its Facts and proof at lines 68, 94, 100-102). 14-36+24=2. The link incidence count yields |W_I| cycle edges and vertices, hence 6 for I={s2,s3} and 4 for I={s1,s3}; these agree with I2(3) and I2(2).
editorial_candidates.uncertainty: A useful optional visual, not a required diagram. The tetrahedron-boundary realization is combinatorial; avoid drawing it as an isometric realization of the spherical metric, whose fundamental triangles have angles pi/3, pi/3, pi/2 (lines 50-52).
